body_html:
Reading a bilingual Bible in English and Spanish is one of the most meaningful ways to grow in both faith and language. Seeing a familiar verse in two languages makes you slow down, notice words you once skimmed and hear Scripture with fresh ears. For bilingual families, it can bring generations together around the same pages. This guide covers how to choose a bilingual Bible, a simple way to read it and some verses to begin with.

Key takeaways
  • A bilingual Bible places English and Spanish translations side by side.
  • Choose translations that match your church tradition and reading level.
  • Read slowly: the goal is understanding and prayer, not speed.
  • Familiar verses are the perfect starting point for Spanish learners.
{{toc}}

Why read a bilingual Bible?

  • It slows you down. Comparing two versions makes you pay attention to every word, which naturally leads to reflection.
  • It reveals nuance. Different languages capture different shades of meaning. A word you skimmed in English may stop you in Spanish.
  • It builds Spanish gently. Because many verses are already familiar, you understand the Spanish easily. That is ideal {{link:comprehensible-input-spanish|comprehensible input}}.
  • It connects families. Parents, grandparents and children who prefer different languages can read and pray together.

Choosing translations for your bilingual Bible

Bilingual Bibles pair one English translation with one Spanish translation. A few you will often see:

Spanish translationNotes
Reina-Valera 1960 (RVR1960)The most widely used Spanish Bible among Protestant churches; traditional, majestic language
Nueva Versión Internacional (NVI)Modern, clear Spanish; easier for learners
La Biblia de las Américas (LBLA)Fairly literal, popular for study
Biblia de Jerusalén, Biblia LatinoamericanaCommon in Catholic communities

On the English side, you may already have a favourite. On this site I quote Scripture in English from the World English Bible, a modern public-domain translation you can read freely at eBible.org.

{{image:2}}

A simple method for reading a bilingual Bible

  1. Pray first. Ask for an open heart. In Spanish: Señor, abre mi corazón a tu Palabra.
  2. Read the verse in your stronger language. Understand it fully.
  3. Read it slowly in the other language, aloud. Notice words that feel different.
  4. Pick one word to sit with. Ask: what does this word add?
  5. Write the verse in both languages. Copying by hand helps memory and meditation.
  6. Close in prayer, perhaps in the language that felt closest today.

Saving verses like this is a faith-filled version of {{link:sentence-mining-spanish|sentence mining}}: you build a personal collection of lines that matter to you.

Verses to start with

John 3:16

“For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.” (John 3:16, WEB)

Porque de tal manera amó Dios al mundo, que ha dado a su Hijo unigénito, para que todo aquel que en él cree, no se pierda, mas tenga vida eterna. (Juan 3:16, RVR1960)

Notice de tal manera, “in such a way”. Spanish emphasizes not only how much God loved, but the manner of that love.

Psalm 23:1

“Yahweh is my shepherd; I shall lack nothing.” (Psalm 23:1, WEB)

Jehová es mi pastor; nada me faltará. (Salmo 23:1, RVR1960)

A beautiful sentence for learners: nada me faltará uses the same structure as me gusta, literally “nothing will be lacking to me”.

Psalm 46:10

“Be still, and know that I am God.” (Psalm 46:10, WEB)

Estad quietos, y conoced que yo soy Dios. (Salmo 46:10, RVR1960)

Estad and conoced are vosotros commands, the plural “you” used in Spain and in traditional Bible Spanish. I explain vosotros in {{link:latin-american-vs-spain-spanish|Latin American vs Spain Spanish}}.

{{book:god-and-you}}

Notes for Spanish learners

  • Traditional translations use older forms. RVR1960 uses words like mas (but) and vosotros commands. Modern versions like the NVI are easier.
  • God’s name appears differently. RVR1960 often uses Jehová, while many modern versions use el Señor.
  • Faith vocabulary is full of cognates: gracia, fe, esperanza, salvación, misericordia. See {{link:english-spanish-cognates|English–Spanish cognates}} for the patterns.
  • Feelings matter. Notice how Scripture uses amar for God’s love, the verb behind te amo.
{{image:3}}

Reading a bilingual Bible as a family

In many bilingual homes, grandparents pray in Spanish while children feel more at home in English. A bilingual Bible lets everyone read the same passage together, each in the language of their heart. Take turns reading a verse in each language, then share one word that stood out. These moments can become cherished family traditions, and they gently support children’s Spanish too; see {{link:raising-bilingual-children-english-spanish|raising bilingual children}} for more ideas.

Faith is one of the deepest places two languages can meet. For the bigger picture of bilingual life, read my complete guide to {{link:bilingual-english-and-spanish|bilingual English and Spanish}}.

A 7-day bilingual reading plan

DayPassageTheme
1Psalm 23God as shepherd
2Matthew 5:1–12The Beatitudes
3John 3:16–17God’s love
4Psalm 46Stillness and trust
51 Corinthians 13What love is
6Matthew 6:9–13The Lord’s Prayer
7Romans 8:38–39Nothing can separate us

Read each passage once in each language, choose one verse to copy and carry it with you through the day. By the end of the week you will have seven verses in two languages, and a new habit of slow, attentive reading.

Final thoughts

A bilingual Bible is not just a language tool. It is an invitation to read slowly, to listen again and to let familiar words surprise you. Start with a verse you already love, read it in both languages and let it stay with you through the day.

faq.q: What is the best Spanish Bible translation?
faq.a: It depends on your tradition and goal. Reina-Valera 1960 is the most widely used among Protestants, the NVI offers modern and easy Spanish, and Catholic readers often use the Biblia de Jerusalén or Biblia Latinoamericana.

faq.q: Can reading the Bible help me learn Spanish?
faq.a: Yes. Because many verses are already familiar, you understand the Spanish easily, which makes Scripture excellent reading practice alongside its spiritual value.

faq.q: Should I read the Spanish or English first?
faq.a: Read first in your stronger language to understand the verse, then slowly in the other language, ideally aloud, to notice new nuances.
